speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
maintopic: WARHEADS AT U.S. BASES IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house of the continental defence arrangement which the government has entered into with the United States government concerning the storage of nuclear warheads in Canada for United States interceptor aircraft stationed in two United States leased bases in Newfoundland. The arrangement which has been concluded was the result of negotiations to which I referred in the house on May 20 and again on June 7. It is in the form of an exchange of notes and specifies the conditions under which nuclear air to air defensive weapons will be stored for United States air force interceptor aircraft under the operational command of the commander in chief of the joint North American air defence command stationed at United States leased bases in Newfoundland.
Under the arrangement operational use of these defensive weapons would be governed by the operational plans of NORAD, approved by both governments. In other respects as well, such as the strict safety measures which will apply, the terms now agreed parallel those relating to the conditions under which warheads will be made available to Canadian forces as announced on August 16. In accordance with the requirements of national security, military details cannot be made public.
This exchange of notes complements that of August 16 relating to Canadian forces in that it will permit all NORAD air defence forces stationed in Canada, regardless of their nationality, to be equipped with weapons
which, it has been agreed, are presently required for them to fulfil effectively their role of protecting this continent against bomber attack. As a result, the Canadian and United States forces assigned to NORAD for the air defence of North America, wherever they are stationed, will have the means at their disposal to discharge their defensive task, a task which we all hope they will never be called upon to perform.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: WARHEADS AT U.S. BASES IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, of course, the house is in the same position as it has continued to be under this government in that the information made available to us is of so sketchy a character as to deny us the opportunity of knowing whether or not, in any agreement entered into, the sovereignty of Canada is protected or whether Canada is placed in a subservient position. Furthermore, it is a matter, I think, of interest to know that during the election campaign the present Prime Minister told us that the Canadian government intended to negotiate itself out of the possession of nuclear weapons or their storage in Canada.
Naturally the house would appreciate the opportunity to learn something of the negotiations, if any, that have gone on, for it strikes me as passing strange that a government that intends to negotiate out of nuclear weapons now places itself in a position where millions of dollars will be expended for the storage of nuclear weapons. At the same time, in the back of its mind, the government intends to bring about by renegotiation the removal of those things that they are now going to expend money upon for storage purposes.

maintopic: WARHEADS AT U.S. BASES IN NEWFOUNDLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the statement which has been made by the Prime Minister simply forges another link in the chain which is now binding Canada to the United States as a military satellite, and is one more step toward making Canada a nuclear power.
We in this group protest most vehemently that these announcements are being made without any documents being placed before parliament and without full knowledge of the facts being made available to hon. members of the house. It seems to us that this agreement ought to be filed in the house, as

Storage of Nuclear Warheads Announced should the agreement with reference to the acquisition of nuclear arms for Canadian forces.
I would urge the Prime Minister first of all to make this information available to the house. If he is not prepared to make it available to the house, he might at least agree to make it available to the parliamentary committee on defence so that the members of that committee would have an opportunity of perusing this information and of questioning the ministers concerned regarding it.
I would also urge that the Prime Minister set aside a day fairly soon for the discussion of this whole question of Canada's becoming a military satellite of the United States or being boxed more and more into a nuclear role, out of which the government itself promised to negotiate us. If the government does not avail itself of such an opportunity, then those of us in the opposition groups would have to take whatever opportunity we can find to raise this question and have it fully debated in the house.

As I stated last Friday, Mr. Speaker, and repeated to the house yesterday, I should like to inform the house of the progress made in the negotiations at Tokyo concerning the north Pacific fisheries treaty, as reported to me by the Canadian delegation which returned to Ottawa last night. I also table, for the information of the house, the press release issued at the close of the Tokyo meetings.
As I informed the house on June 24, the negotiations between Canada, Japan and the United States on the north Pacific fisheries convention commenced in Washington, D.C., on June 6 and recessed on June 21 after a useful exchange of views. At the close of the Washington meetings, Canada and the United States believed that the conservation and rational development of the north Pacific fisheries would be assured best by continuation of the present conventions embodying the abstention principle. Japan, on the other hand,

proposed a new convention omitting that principle but providing for joint conservation measures by the three countries.
The negotiations were resumed in Tokyo on September 16. At the opening session I emphasized Canada's concern for the protection of our salmon, halibut and herring fisheries in the north Pacific. Canada, in co-operation with the United States, has maintained these fisheries at highly productive levels through extensive research and strict regulation of our own fishing and, in the case of salmon, through measures to protect and assist their production in our fresh waters. These fisheries are fully utilized by our fishermen and should be reserved for their use. On the other hand, Canada wants protection for these fisheries with minimum interference with Japan's use of other fish stocks not now fully exploited.
In the course of the Tokyo meetings, the United States presented a modification of the draft convention proposed by Japan in Washington. Discussions are proceeding on the basis of this draft which would provide the necessary protection for our fisheries but without explicit statement of the abstention principle as it appears in the present convention.
The negotiations were most productive and greatly improved the understanding by each country of the interests and positions of the others. It was especially promising to discover the high degree of protection for our fisheries which Japan is prepared to afford under a new convention. The meeting recessed to enable the delegations to consult further with their governments, but with a feeling of optimism regarding agreement on a mutually satisfactory convention. It is hoped that this will be accomplished at the next series of meetings which, the conference recommended, should be reconvened next spring. The Canadian delegation expressed the hope that these meetings could be held in Ottawa.
The differences which remain to be resolved are concerned mainly with the manner in which the basis for protection of these fisheries is expressed in the new convention. In the case of salmon the Canadian position is that the convention must recognize Canada's special interest in the stocks which spawn in our rivers, based on long continued scientific management and full utilization, and also on positive cultural measures and restrictions of other water uses damaging to salmon production. In the case of halibut the joint special interest of the United States and Canada should also be explicitly recognized in view of the restoration of the fishery to highly productive levels by effective study and regulation by the international Pacific halibut commission.
North Pacific Treaty Negotiations
Canada's special interest in our intensively fished herring stocks should also be recognized. We want the basis for our special interest in these fisheries to be so expressed in the convention as to give general and continuing protection. It is still necessary to reconcile this objective with Japan's reluctance to include any statement of principles which might hinder the development of her far-flung fisheries. Nevertheless the reasonable and constructive tone of the discussions gives hope for eventual agreement. In the meantime the present convention remains in force.
As I have indicated before, when any agreements are reached they will be fully discussed before the standing committee on marine and fisheries before final acceptance by the government.

Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the reason the treaty negotiations have been adjourned is because Japan is really not interested in having a treaty on the north Pacific fisheries which contains the abstention principle. It may well be in the interests of Japan not to have such a treaty, but it is certainly in the interests of the other fishing countries of the north Pacific, Canada, the United States and the Soviet union.
We believe that Japan has been encouraged in its opposition to a treaty by what we consider the weak positions taken by the governments of both Canada and the United States over the past two years. This spring the government of Canada acted with undue haste, and I think with irregular procedure, in agreeing that Japan be allowed to fish for herring and halibut in areas from which it was formerly excluded. We think the Canadian government has taken an apologetic attitude, both before and during these negotiations. Our delegation seems to be fighting a rearguard action against the demands of Japan, but it should not be afraid to state that we intend to protect our very great investment in conservation against exploitation by other countries.

Has the government given any assistance to the Beaverhouse Indians resident near Dobie, Ontario, and, if so (a) what assistance towards education has been provided and (b) what other assistance has been provided?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
The group is known as the Beaverhouse lake Indians and reside in the general area of Dobie, Indian point and Beaverhouse lake, Ontario. There is no Indian reserve in that area and with a few exceptions, all members of the group are of nonIndian status. The few persons of Indian status residing in this area are self supporting and no assistance from the Department of Citizenship and Immigration has been required.
With respect to Indian health services, the isolation of the area, the difficult travel conditions and the small Indian population make regular medical coverage impractical. Emergency medical care, when required, is provided and all registered Indians are insured under the Ontario hospital services commission.

Has the government given any assistance to the Indian band located at Matachewan, Ontario, and, if so (a) what assistance has been provided towards education, and (b) what other assistance has been provided?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
1. (a) These Indians reside in the town of Matachewan and not on an Indian reserve. Their children have been attending public and high schools in the district which they are entitled to do as residents and accordingly no educational assistance has been provided by the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
(b) Notwithstanding the fact that these Indians reside off the reserve, relief assistance in the amount of $1,379.93 in 1961-62 and $3,553.50 in 1962-63 was provided to various members of this group. In 1959 the department purchased a number of trap lines for the Matachewan Indians. These were in addition to those set aside for this band under the Ontario fur agreement. Assistance was also provided to this band to commence logging

operations on the Matachewan Indian reserve and in the placement of Indians in employment, particularly in the forest industry.
In so far as the Department of National Health and Welfare is concerned, an Indian health services public health nurse visits the village every six to eight weeks. A Red Cross nurse is stationed in the village. The nurses refer cases requiring a higher level of treatment to a designated physician at Kirkland Lake. The department pays for care provided to Indians on a fee for service basis. Transportation of the patient is usually at departmental expense. All registered Indians are insured under the Ontario hospital services commission.

speechtext:
Has the government secured an agreement with the United States government that Canada shall have a recognized exemption from the 15 per cent tax proposed by the Kennedy administration on the purchases by American citizens of foreign securities; and, if so, (a) what are the terms of such exemption (b) will a copy of the signed agreement be tabled in the house?
Answer: The agreement with the United States government that Canada shall have a recognized exemption from the 15 per cent tax proposed by the Kennedy administration on the purchases by American citizens of foreign securities is contained in the communique of July 21, 1963, agreed between representatives of Canada and the United States.
Ottawa, July 21, 1963: Hon. Walter L. Gordon, Minister of Finance, issued this afternoon the following statement which had been agreed between representatives of Canada and United States meeting in Washington during the week end: 28902-5-214$
Questions
"Representatives of Canada and the United States met during the week end to appraise the impact on the Canadian financial markets of the proposed United States "interest equalization tax".
The two governments recognized the need for effective action to improve the balance of payments position of both countries and are both equally determined that such action shall not impair the intimate economic relationships between the two countries, nor impede the growth essential for both economies.
For many years the capital markets of the two countries have been closely interconnected, and United States exports of capital to Canada have financed a substantial portion of the Canadian current account deficit with the U.S. This need continues. A portion of these flows must be supplied through the sale of new issues of Canadian securities in American markets. U.S. officials had considered that ample flows for these needs would continue under the proposed "interest equalization tax". However, Canadian representatives stated that this would require a very substantial rise m the entire Canadian interest rate structure. It was recognized by both governments that such a development would be undesirable in present economic circumstances.
In the light of this situation U.S. officials agreed that the draft legislation to be submitted to the congress would include a provision authorizing a procedure under which the president could modify the application of the tax by the establishment from time to time of exemptions, which he could make either unlimited or limited in amount. The President would thus have the flexibility to permit tax free purchases of new issues needed to maintain the unimpeded flow of trade and payments between the two countries, and to take care of exceptional situations that might arise in the case of other countries. U.S. officials made clear that this did not modify their proposals regarding the taxation of transactions in outstanding securities; over the past year such transactions between Canada and the U.S. have not been a major factor.
The Canadian authorities stated that it would not be the desire or intention of Canada to increase her foreign exchange reserves through the proceeds of borrowings in the United States, and it is the hope and expectation of both governments that by maintaining close consultation it will prove possible in practice to have an unlimited exemption for Canada without adverse effect on the United States.
It was agreed that active consultations would continue to strengthen the close economic relations between the two countries and at the same time facilitate measures for making the maximum practicable contributions to economic expansion and the strength and stability of both currencies."

Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege affecting the business of the house, Your Honour has been concerned about the length of the question period upon calling the orders of the day. Nearly every day ministers are telling us that some of the questions asked would be better put on the order paper. I should like to draw the attention of the leader of the house to the fact that there are questions on the order paper which have been there since the first week of July. One of them, the very first question, was there on July 2 and it requires simply a yes or no answer. Certainly if you want to discourage members from putting questions on the order paper, the easiest way to do it is to leave the questions there for three months. Hon. members will then have no recourse but to ask them on orders of the day. It seems to me that some review of the questions should be made by the leader of the house in order to speed up answers.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the placing of the maritime transportation unions of Canada under the management and control of trustees; to provide for the establishment of the board of trustees of the maritime transportation unions consisting of a chairman and two other members; to provide for the payment of their remuneration and expenses and to authorize the employment and remuneration of such personnel as may be necessary for the carrying out of the duties and powers of the trustees under the said measure.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Lamoureux in the chair.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in introducing this resolution I would remind the members of the house of the statement I made on August 1, the day before adjournment. On that occasion I announced the decision of the government to establish a trusteeship to deal with the critical maritime shipping situation affecting trade, labour and other international relations between Canada and the United States.
It will be recalled that Mr. Justice Norris delivered his recommendations in mid July of this year, following what I described at the time as one of the most intensive inquiries
[Mr. Douglas.)
ever made in Canada in a labour relations situation. Justice Norris' report has received praise throughout Canada. There has been some criticism as well. In commenting on the latter, I have said the facts of the report speak for themselves, and that no detailed challenge has been made which goes to the basis of the facts as they were established before the commission.
When I announced the government's decision in respect of the trusteeship, as recommended by the commissioner, I said the government would proceed with legislation to provide for such a trusteeship when the house reconvened, unless an effective alternative were found in the meantime. I informed the house in August that the proposed action was supported by four of the five unions directly involved and by the Canadian Labour Congress. It is a matter of record also that spokesmen for all the other parties in the house strongly endorsed the decision of the government in this regard. Naturally, Mr. Chairman, I am grateful to hon. members for this support.
Since August, and more particularly during the past three weeks, some criticism has been directed at a public trusteeship, and pressure has been generated both in Canada and the United States for a voluntary form of trusteeship. The latter has been urged as being in the best tradition of free unions, and as being consistent with the sound development of international unions in Canada and the United States over the past 100 years.
Everyone agrees a private arrangement, whereby union organizations themselves establish controls over their own members and institutions, is the desirable and preferable way to proceed, provided this would end the disruption of shipping and restore clean and democratic unionism where this is lacking in the water transportation industry.
In view of this position which we in the government have maintained throughout, and in view of the strong representations received in this connection, we have since August explored exhaustively and continuously the possibility of an effective alternative, while at the same time proceeding with the task of preparing trusteeship legislation so as to be ready for prompt action if all possibility of action by unions themselves failed.
Immediately after the house recessed on August 2, the deputy minister of my department, Mr. Haythorne, went to Washington to discuss the whole situation with Secretary of Labour, Willard Wirtz. This was followed by other direct discussions involving members of the government and departmental officers with members of the United States government and their officers. In addition there has been almost daily contact by telephone and

telegram with United States authorities, either directly or through our embassy in Washington.
Hon. members will also know that the United States Secretary of Labour came to Canada for a second time on September 11 following the deplorable dynamiting of the vessel, Howard L. Shaw, at Chicago.
There have, of course, been numerous discussions throughout the period with officials of the Canadian Labour Congress, and it is also well known that officials of the Canadian Labour Congress have visited Washington from time to time to establish a meeting of minds with U.S. labour officials.
More recently on September 28 I discussed the situation with the U.S. Secretary of Labour in Boston with representatives of the A.F.L.-C.I.O., the C.L.C. and our respective officials. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has also discussed the matter with the U.S. secretary of state during a recent visit to Washington.
In all of these discussions a determined effort has been made to find an acceptable alternative approach to a public trusteeship which would restore union rights to thousands of Canadian seamen as well as ensure, along with that action, freedom of passage of Canadian vessels in United States waters and ports without fear of harassment and violence.
It has not proved possible to secure full agreement of the union leaders in our two countries to such an alternative approach. While it will be clear to all hon. members that the government has never wished to close the door to voluntary settlement, it must under the circumstances now proceed with the legislation.
There has been speculation as to the reception some union leaders in the United States might give to a trusteeship approved by parliament, and even a fear has been expressed in some quarters that a total boycott might be directed against all Canadian maritime shipping in United States ports. Any such reaction would be a grave concern to the government of Canada and all Canadians. It could only result in a serious disturbance to friendly relations between the peoples of our two countries, and I am sure no one wants that. But, no Canadian can accept a state of affairs whereby labour problems, subject to and settled under Canadian law, are exported to another country in an attempt to set aside due process of law in Canada.
The government of Canada can take action to deal with those matters which are under Canadian authority. With respect to violence or other acts of harassment in the United States, we must rely on the good offices and co-operation of the United States government and of responsible union leaders who believe
Maritime Transportation Unions in and are committed to the support of the civil rights of union members and the maintenance of clean and democratic unionism.
A labour union in Canada, whether it is national or international, is free to pursue all legal acts in conducting its business in Canada. It must, however, not seek to flout and disregard Canadian law through attempting to export or transfer Canadian problems, already settled in Canada, to another country for extra-legal determination.
There is a matter of the rights of Canada involved in this situation that transcends the desire of any organization to be dominant in an industry at all costs and regardless of all law.
I would ask hon. members of the committee to give their support to this resolution in the knowledge that we are facing, and may face in the future, a potentially dangerous situation, a difficult situation which cannot be allowed to persist. I ask them to realize with me that the situation may in fact grow worse before it gets better, and I would strongly urge all union members and others concerned with this situation, in both Canada and the United States, to lend their assistance and support to the action which the government, and I feel sure the committee, consider must be taken at this time.
It is my profound hope that through this action we shall see a return to the democratic, free and constructive unionism that is essential to the well-being of labour in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the remarks on behalf of this party will be made by the hon. member for Ontario, and I rise merely for the purpose of asking a question. Under all the circumstances, would the minister feel free at this time on the resolution stage to give the committee a preview of the bill itself-a general summary of it? Ordinarily that is not done but we are endeavouring to assist in passing this legislation, and it would be most helpful for the discussion and would reduce very considerably the time taken on this matter if the minister did feel constrained to give this information.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am willing to co-operate in that suggestion. Maybe I cannot give the information as clearly as it is given in the bill itself, but, with the consent of the committee I will say, the purpose of the bill is to establish a trusteeship of three members to be entrusted with the management and control of the Canadian maritime transportation unions.
The schedule to the bill provides that all the five unions and their maritime locals will be covered by this trusteeship. The authority of the trustees will be the authority that is normally vested in the officers of these
3372	HOUSE OF
Maritime Transportation Unions trade unions by their constitutions and bylaws, except that certain additional powers are given to the trustees, including the appointment of advisory committees of seamen and joint committees of seamen and employers to advise the trustees; the appointment by the trustees of negotiating committees to bargain; advice to the members for prospective changes in the constitutions of the unions; and also authority to remove and suspend officers and employees of any union and provide alternatives in their place. Certain action is taken to place in the hands of the trusteeship the business affairs of the union, but I would rather leave that until we come to the details of the bill. We have placed a provision in the bill that this will be of a temporary character. It will be, I think, for a period of five years; this period has been selected for obvious reasons. There is also a provision that if it is advisable, in the opinion of the trustees, the unions may be removed from the trusteeship and the trusteeship may end before the expiry date. We made an effort to provide a terminal date and make it a temporary and not a permanent arrangement that would continue, once the situation had been cleared up. Those, in general terms, are the provisions of the bill.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I thank the minister.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to make some remarks in respect of this resolution. I do not intend to make any further remarks during the passage of the bill after I have concluded at this time, unless after careful perusal of the provisions of the bill it is thought necessary to deal with some of its provisions or lack of provisions. This situation on the great lakes is a struggle between Mr. Banks, his lieutenants, his aides, and the bona fide labour movement in this country. It is not a struggle, in effect, between the membership of the S.I.U. and others; it is a struggle between Hal Banks, his lieutenants, and the labour movement of this country. I say this because many of the members of the S.I.U. are good Canadians, but they have been held down and exploited by the leadership of the seafarers international union. There was also, and had been for some time ever since the entry of Mr. Banks into this country, an amiable situation existing between the Liberal government of that day and Mr. Banks. This was very forcefully pointed out by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition when he spoke in this house on Friday last. Evidence of this and the expectation of Mr. Banks that this prolonged amiable friendship with the former Liberal government would be projected to the present government has been set out very effectively.


I want to refer to a press clipping from the Toronto Globe and Mail of recent date in which it was said:
Minutes filed before the Norris inquiry by the S.I.U. said the union got along well with former labour minister Milton Gregg, a Liberal, but not so well with the current minister, Michael Starr, a Conservative.
Mr. Banks was looking forward, as I pointed out, to the continuation of that amiable relationship, because in the speech in Washington after the federal election of 1963 he made a statement to the effect that he could not get along with the former minister of labour, meaning myself, but looked forward to more friendly relations with the present, the new Liberal administration. So much for this-

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: So much for politics.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: A terrible thing, politics.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
-friendship. That friendship has now come to an end with the introduction of this resolution and the bill that will follow. But let us look back for a brief moment to the events that have transpired up to the moment. The Norris commission was set up at the behest and the demand of the Canadian Labour Congress because the situation on the great lakes was intolerable. It is obvious to everyone that no government could impose such an inquiry on unions without great criticism from the labour movement in Canada unless it were done at their request. The labour movement is suspicious of moves of this kind, and unless and until they themselves feel the time is ripe for such an inquiry governments cannot move in this direction. It was the former government which moved in this direction. This inquiry was set up with Mr. Justice Norris as the commissioner. He did an excellent job after a long and careful study of the problems and after going into the various aspects of the trouble on the great lakes. Then he made his report. The revelations in that report were such that they shook the whole nation and demands for immediate action on his recommendations were pouring into Ottawa from every part of our country.
This was when the present government began to delay action on the report. The recess was called for parliament. No action was taken. At that time-and I repeat what the Leader of the Opposition said last Friday-we were given assurances that if anything untoward happened during that period of recess, parliament would be called to deal with the situation. The dynamiting of a ship took place. Well, it seemed to be of no consequence to this government. Parliament was not called. Then when we get back here

again we find we are in the second week of this parliament before the resolution is brought forward.
What has transpired in the meantime? One can probably contemplate on this and look into the crystal ball, because we have not been given the facts. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the government was looking for a way out, other than implementing the recommendations made by Mr. Justice Norris. Also, they were trying to bring into their orbit help from wherever they could find it. They went to Washington. They may have suggested that Mr. Wirtz come to Canada and look for some other solution to the problem in this country. Mr. Wirtz came to Canada and, as reported in the newspapers, upon questioning as to what could be done in respect of this matter, he said:
I would rather answer that a little obliquely.
I am a great believer that in the free labour movement there are the elements for dealing with a situation of this kind. I hope very much that some way will be found whereby the assertion of this basic responsibility of free trade unions in this country and in the United States will produce an answer to this.
He also said, as reported in the New York Times, a clipping of which I have here:
I think we believe in both countries that whatever can be done privately is much better done privately than done publicly.
This seed was planted. Then the movement was made to try to find some solution other than that recommended. They even went so far in the last, dying moments as to send the under secretary of labor, Mr. Reynolds, here to see whether a last ditch stand could be taken to find a solution. But all in vain.
The government has now been forced to take the action that they should have taken last July. The Canadian Labour Congress, a responsible body of representatives of the free Canadian labour movement, were probably forced to look into the situation. They knew very well that they could not work out an agreement with the United States unions because of the attacks by the leaders of that movement in the United States upon the leaders of the Canadian Labour Congress. They knew their attitude was such that would bring about no solution. In the release yesterday of the Canadian Labour Congress they advise the people of this country:
The executive council of the Canadian Labour Congress, meeting in Ottawa, today decided to inform the government that repeated efforts to effect a voluntary method of cleaning up the union situation on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway have been unsuccessful. We are therefore unable to make any recommendation regarding a private trusteeship.
Mr. Chairman, let us look to see what their attitude is with respect to this situation. They say:
Maritime Transportation Unions -the intolerable situation which currently exists has to be corrected. Everything humanly possible has been done by the congress and its affiliates to resolve the problem without government intervention. Unfortunately, the other trade unions could not be convinced to co-operate.
They mean those in the United States.
In view of this failure and the position of the affiliates involved, all four of which have indicated that they are prepared to accept temporary government trusteeship-
So that the government has eventually been forced to take action which they could have taken last July, because even then it was evident that no other solution could solve this problem.
However, when this trusteeship is set up and goes to work there remains a very difficult problem with respect to shipping on the great lakes. The harassment of Canadian ships which has been experienced in the past will be redoubled in the future, not only in United States ports but in other ports. The Minister of Labour mentioned that the Secretary of State for External Affairs took up this matter in Washington. I refer to a clipping from the Toronto Telegram dated September 9 which says:
The U.S. department of labour called on the F.B.I. to investigate this latest flare-up in the union war on the great lakes. But in Chicago the F.B.I. said "We're taking no action at present." Secretary of state Rusk labelled it "an unfortunate incident".
This refers to the dynamiting of a Canadian ship in a Chicago port. Secretary of state Rusk labels it "an unfortunate incident". No action was taken. The report goes on:
An official said the state department would want to hear the F.B.I.'s findings but added: "There is very little that this department can do."
Canada's external affairs minister Martin complained to Mr. Rusk over lunch here Saturday.
The minister did not ask or demand that something be done; he complained to Mr. Rusk over lunch. This is the method of approach of this government with respect to this very serious situation.
The timing was unfortunate. Minutes before the two statesmen had exchanged compliments about 150 years of peace along the U.S.-Canadian border. Mr. Rusk handed over an ugly big woodcarving to mark the anniversary of the last great lakes battle-lake Erie, 1813.
No action has been taken in the United States to deal with this matter. The courts there have issued injunctions. These injunctions have been completely ignored and no action taken to put them into effect. We must look at this situation seriously and not just go and discuss over lunch what happened on the great lakes in 1813. The happenings now on the great lakes are far more important and far more dangerous to Canada. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, as has been
3374	HOUSE OF
Maritime Transportation Unions stated, complained about the matter. I think that we should make strong demands, in order to bring about peace on the great lakes, that the United States government take some strong, effective measures to see that Canadian ships are able to arrive at United States ports and load and unload their cargoes without harassment such as that experienced in recent months.
I must point out that the setting up of a trusteeship is not something that a Canadian labour movement or any labour movement likes to have happen. It is very distasteful to the labour movement. But I think that all who are affected by this will realize that it is probably the only solution to the problem. I want to point out to the government that this trusteeship should be on a temporary basis. There should be some clear understanding that the trusteeship should have this matter cleaned up by spring, before the season on the great lakes opens again. It should certainly be underlined that this should not be taken as a precedent to sustain the present situation in the labour movement in Canada; that it will not be a practice of government to put unions under a trusteeship unless the situation warrants it, or the position is as serious as that which has been experienced recently on the great lakes. I fully realize the fear which the Canadian Labour Congress and other unions across this country have with respect to this action, and consequently I think their fears should be allayed by a statement from the government to the effect that it is not setting a precedent, and that this trusteeship is of a temporary nature.
We will look closely, Mr. Chairman, at the legislation when it comes before us, and we will examine it to see whether it is effective and workable. I hope the members of the house will find their way clear to pass this legislation as quickly as possible.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my remarks will be confined to the principles involved in this resolution, and to the situation which has existed for the past number of months on the great lakes as it concerns, in particular, the S.I.U. In approaching this legislation I believe it is the first duty of this house to grasp clearly the depth and the importance of the issues which are involved. The legislation is the last step in a long chain of events, a continuous story of violence, disruption of commerce, defiance of law and exploitation of seamen on the great lakes. This has continued for many years and it has culminated in the formation of the Canadian maritime union, numerous acts of violence against its members and, finally, a retaliatory boycott of S.I.U. ships on the Welland canal by members of the C.B.R.T. This is what precipitated the inquiry held by Mr. Justice Norris, and the recommendations which we are now asked to pass into law.
No one who has read the report of Mr. Justice Norris-and I believe this report gives us the true facts of the case as they would have been found had one judge or 50 sat on this royal commission-can have any doubt whatsoever as to the basic issues involved. We are dealing with the issue of the preservation of law and order as against mob violence. We are asked to restrain a man who, according to the commission's report, is lawless and prepared to use any weapon to gain his own ends. The commission has found a grisly tale of the exploitation of Canadian citizens, financially and economically, by the dictatorial legal and extra-legal powers assumed by the management of the S.I.U. There is not the least shadow of doubt that the management of this union has been directly responsible for instigating violence against the persons and property of those, particularly the members of the new Canadian maritime union, who threatened its monopoly of power.
There is not one law in this country for citizens who live inland, and another law for

the waterfront. It is the duty of this government-of this parliament, ultimately-to make sure that the Queen's justice and the Queen's peace extend to every part of this dominion and, yes, integrity and honesty in both labour and commercial operations. Dishonesty by consent, whether by the S.I.U. or the C.S.L. is wrong. Extraordinary situations arise, and extraordinary measures such as those proposed today are needed to deal with them. But unless we regard the maintenance of simple law and order within our nation as the first and the highest duty of government, we are failing the citizens of this country whom we represent, in the most elemental duties of government.
The second major issue with which we are dealing is that of the position of the Canadian workingman. There is not the least shadow of doubt, as one studies the Norris report, that it is the Canadian seaman who has been the real sufferer in this affair. It is he who has been charged the excessive initiation fees. It is his money that has gone into the welfare funds of the union, funds for which no proper accounting has been made. It is he who has found his bread and his livelihood taken away at the whim of a dictatorial union boss with a criminal record; it is he who has been beaten up, or has found himself on the infamous "do not ship" list, should he have dared to defy the power of this dictator. Let us remember that it is we ourselves-the parliament of Canada itself-who have approved the legislation under which the S.I.U. has been operating, and this includes the right to make collective bargaining agreements which compel all sailors employed on ships manned by the union to belong to it. When such abuses as these are found to exist, we must examine the legislation itself under which we have allowed the union to operate, to see if it is entirely free from blame.
The third issue that confronts us is the future of the labour movement itself in Canada, as a body independent of control from outside the country. This is raised squarely by the issues in this case, and we must face it squarely. The Canadian maritime union was created through efforts of the Canadian Labour Congress as a Canadian answer to the corruption of a foreign controlled international union. On its creation, something approaching open warfare broke out, a situation to which the government of the day appears to have turned a blind eye until compelled by the blocking of the Welland canal to take some action. Government inaction continued for too long, in spite of repeated protests to the Department of Labour, which placed the government of the day in full possession of the facts of the case. Unless the power of the S.I.U. is
Maritime Transportation Unions curbed; unless the principle is established that Canadians have the effective, practical right, fully guaranteed by effective enforcement of law, to form unions of their own and conduct their union affairs peaceably and without interference, we may as well confess that an independent Canadian labour movement is at an end, that from now on the activities of Canadian workers will be controlled from outside the country. We will be forced to confess that we can no longer control for ourselves the labour conditions of our own Canadian citizens, that we have allowed them to pass from our own control to that of gangster-dominated foreign unions, exploiting our workers for their own advantage. This is a situation that is perilously close, unless the government acts with decision at this time.
There are two key factors in deciding the course of action that the government proposes. The first of these is the element of time. The navigation season on the seaway can be expected to close in less than two months from now. The cost to ship owners of having their vessels tied up beyond that date is heavy. This is a fact well known to those concerned in this dispute. Time is on the side of the existing union management. The longer the delay in having the S.I.U. placed under effective control, the greater the bargaining power of that union in dictating its demands to ship owners. Two months have gone by while parliament has been in recess and this legislation has been in preparation. Freeze-up is approaching. There is no room for pussyfooting. Action, immediate action, is necessary now.
There is no ground for giving these powers to the government if, as some reports indicate, it is the government's intention to delay making use of the legislation once it has been obtained. Delay is only going to make matters worse. This situation has been deteriorating season after season and it will continue until resolute action is taken. We cannot waste any more time.
The second key quality which I demand be shown by the government here is courage. Let us keep our basic sense of what is right and what is wrong in such a situation as we are facing now. The law has been defied and the rights of Canadian citizens have been shamefully disregarded. A royal commission has put us in possession of the facts. It has made this key recommendation of trusteeship which has now been embodied in legislation. There is only one thing which remains to be done, and that can be spelled out in a single word-action. Are we going to enforce peace, honesty and the law in this matter or not? To say that we are not, to allow defiance of the law and the principles of justice to

Maritime Transportation Unions continue because of lack of courage on our part would certainly be an abandonment of the responsibilities we have to the Canadian people as their representatives in this house. Heaven knows, we follow the example of the United States in a lot of things, but for once let us have the courage to show that we in Canada can take action that will protect our citizens and maintain the law, about which we talk so much.
We have seen a Canadian ship, the Howard L. Shaw, tied up in a United States port for the whole of the summer. We have seen how this ship has been boycotted, abused, even dynamited. The Prime Minister has made complaints directly to the President of the United States in the matter. The owners of the ship have reported they have suffered a loss of something more than $3 million in endeavouring to assert their right to man their ships with crews belonging to a Canadian union. Court orders and court injunctions have been obtained and have proved to be not worth the paper on which they were written. The law and the executive have been defied. The word of the union boss on the Chicago waterfront is stronger than the word of the courts of the United States or its president. Perhaps this is good enough for the United States, but I believe it rests upon us as Canadians to insist on something better so far as our own country is concerned.
We as members of this House of Commons must realize that there is a great deal at stake, and certainly this is not an easy matter. The Banks problem would not be nearly so acute were it not for the key position that Banks himself holds as the man who controls a large block of Canadian votes, which are a matter of expediency to the international union in the United States. There is in the United States a conflict between the eastern and western elements of the S.I.U., and the leadership of the S.I.U. itself is an important factor in the control of other groups of unions in the United States. Banks through his Canadian votes as a non-citizen of this country holds this balance of power in the labour union struggle that is going on in the United States.
It is for this reason that I would point out to the Minister of Labour and the government that I believe the government would have been running an unwarranted risk if they had allowed any form of private trusteeship to take place. Perhaps it is not possible for us to say with any degree of supporting evidence that the very forces that have permitted this situation to develop and continue in Canada are responsible for the strike we

have on the St. Lawrence waterfront, but certainly the facts of the situation would indicate that they are.
We must have a guarantee that justice will be maintained and that the rights of Canadian citizens will be protected. We can only do that in this extreme situation on the basis of a government trusteeship. There must be a guarantee that Banks will not still be able to pull the wires and control affairs from the other side of the border. The only way we can be positively sure of complete integrity will be if the functions of the management of the Canadian branch of the S.I.U. are placed under the direction of a government trusteeship.
We in the Social Credit party are convinced that such action must be taken and taken quickly. Let us remember that the Canadian Labour Congress has willingly agreed to submit to such a government trusteeship, and even after the congress has been given the opportunity to try to work out something on a private basis it has come back and said that the situation is hopeless. Thus the Canadian Labour Congress is behind the trusteeship and is supporting it. At least, those unions in the congress that are not dictated to from the United States support it, because we know that pressure from across the border on the part of some other international unions has been brought to bear upon the Minister of Labour and the government to avoid taking the very action which is being recommended now. If a union that has nothing to hide expresses its willingness to be placed under trusteeship, why should we hesitate to impose this on a union whose record shows clearly that it is corrupt and completely gangster dominated.
Finally, I believe that this legislation is the necessary first step, but it is not the end of the affairs about which we are now talking because there are ramifications which go much farther. This legislation can and must be a temporary matter-we agree on that- because we must straighten out a situation that cannot otherwise be controlled. But after the trusteeship is imposed I believe it is of the utmost importance that a committee of the house go thoroughly into the legislation under which unions operate in this country at the present time, to make sure that the legislation is in the best interests of those it is designed to protect, Canadian workingmen.
It is quite plain that much of the excessive power that a union has over its members arises from a right that the union is given by federal statute law, the right to impose a closed shop agreement within a bargaining unit so that only union members can obtain employment. Let us recognize that, although the right of a workingman to strike against

his employer is always to be jealously defended as one of labour's precious rights, a closed shop such as the S.I.U. has imposed is in fact an effective device to remove all power from a worker to exercise his right to strike against his own union management.
This is a very fundamental point. The worker is treated not as an intelligent citizen with the power to make his own decisions but as a commodity for sale on the labour market. This is exactly what the S.I.U. has been doing through the right it apparently assumes under our existing legislation of hiring and firing workers on the great lakes ships.
The profit from the monopoly of labour that flows from such a position has been going, not to the workers themselves but to the corrupt labour boss who stands as a broker between the workingman and the employer who wants to make use of his services, charging each side the maximum that the market will bear for his own selfish interests. Such a monopoly is even able to force a company like The Canada Steamship Lines into dishonesty, by consent, which results in the perpetuation and expansion of the very thing against which the working people of Canada should have protection.
We, the parliament of Canada, have established the laws that permit such a situation. I suggest respectfully to the government that the next step they must take in this matter, when the trusteeship has been set up, is to refer the Canada Shipping Act and other federal legislation involving the rights and privileges of labour to the appropriate committee of the house so that the effective working of this legislation, in the light of the interests of Canadian citizens, can be thoroughly reviewed, particularly in the light of the events which have developed during the last couple of years.
I am also extremely concerned about one recommendation made by Mr. Justice Norris in his report, which appears to be that the trusteeship should be imposed for the purpose of integrating the unions on which the trusteeship is imposed. I should like to question whether the government considers it a legitimate fact that a government trusteeship should be used to influence the actual union organization that exists in this area. I do not think it is. I would suggest that this part of the Norris report be questioned very seriously because I am convinced this is an interference with the individual rights of the workingman.
A trade union is not an organization that should be started, directed or controlled by government, except in the case of most flagrant abuse, an example of which we now have in the case of the S.I.U. Both the government and members of the opposition
Maritime Transportation Unions should be well aware by now of the blunder they made in permitting Hal Banks to take charge of the Canadian waterfront. Directed labour and directed labour organizations, belong in Soviet Russia or communist China, not in a free country such as Canada.
The purpose of this legislation, then, is quite simply to ensure respect for Canadian law and to protect Canadian seamen from the abuses to which their union has subjected them. It is no more than that. It will only be making a bad situation worse if the trustees, themselves, begin to make organizational decisions which interfere with the free run of an association of Canadian citizens and union members.
These are the basic reasons, Mr. Chairman, for our support of this legislation. At the same time, we caution the government that their responsibility under this legislation is twofold. First of all, it is to protect the rights of our Canadian workingmen from a union which has become corrupt, which is oppressing them. The other responsibility is to maintain justice, which it is our responsibility to maintain for every Canadian citizen. Beyond that we must not interfere with individual rights which belong to each of us, whether or not we choose to belong to a union of workingmen.
When the legislation is introduced, I am confident that all of us in this house will face up to these responsibilities, and will not think in terms of five years, although five years may be necessary to make a blanket coverage for any eventuality that may occur. However, I am sure we will quickly once again permit normal operations to continue in the great lakes shipping area and on the St. Lawrence, and at the same time protect the Canadian workingman who works as a seaman on the various shipping lines operating in this area.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, as one who has had a long association with trade unions, the idea of a public trusteeship is very naturally repugnant to me. But I propose to support this legislation because I deem it to be an extraordinary measure to meet an extraordinary situation. The question which the parliament of Canada faces is not whether we want a public trusteeship but rather what other alternative is there, in the light of the appalling situation which obtains in the maritime shipping industry of Canada?
In order to see the situation which does obtain, may I just briefly review a few of the facts. Hal C. Banks was brought to Canada in 1949 with the co-operation of the government, the trades and labour congress of Canada and the shipping companies on the great lakes in order to displace the Canadian
