Maritime Transportation Unions seamen's union which, it was claimed, was a communist dominated union. In 1952 Banks applied lor status as a landed immigrant. His application was rejected by the department of immigration on the grounds he had a criminal record in the United States. He appealed this decision to the minister of immigration, and in June, 1954, an order in council was passed giving him the status of a landed immigrant. In 1958 he applied for full citizenship. This application was rejected by Mr. Justice Lafon-taine.
Banks and the S.I.U. were not long in operation until it became apparent that Banks was building a hoodlum empire based on intimidation, extortion and lawlessness. First, he destroyed democratic control of the S.I.U. Second, he conspired with some of the shipping companies to illegally break the existing collective bargaining agreements which those companies had with properly certified trade unions. Third, Banks and the S.I.U. used lawless tactics in an attempt to destroy other unions in order to extend the membership of the S.I.U. I think a reading of the Norris report makes it quite clear that the blame for this intolerable situation falls on three separate groups.
It falls, first of all, of course on the S.I.U. and its president who instituted a reign of terror on the waterfront. There were the "do not ship" lists and the hiring halls by which Banks had control of whether or not any man would be able to get a job, and how long he would keep it. There was the control of the pension fund, which he mismanaged as the record will show. There was the fact that, with the consent of the Canadian government and the companies, the men's vacation pay was turned over to the S.I.U. and not to the men. I think the record shows that some $300,000 of that has never been distributed to the seamen. This gave him control of the union so that democracy was steadily destroyed. First, the blame lies with Banks and his organization.
The second share of blame lies with the shipping companies, at least the majority of them, and particularly Canada Steamship Lines who were in collusion with Banks and who, by working with Banks, sought to gain competitive advantage over the other shipping companies. I should say that credit should be given to the Upper Lakes Shipping Company and to its president Mr. Jack Leitch who, according to the Norris report, stood up almost alone against the depredations of Banks and the union. As a matter of fact, I probably should just document that by referring to page 41 of the report where the commissioner says:
The Canada Steamship Lines and its affiliates, with their diverse interests and integrated operation in many fields tributary to the business of


lake transport, found it easy to make accommodations with Hal C. Banks and his union

the S.I.U. of Canada-and did not suffer from union action. Other lake shipping companies, if they wished to survive, had to fall in line and accept the terms arranged between C.S.L. and Banks regardless of their own situation. The resulting tendency was to deprive the public of the benefit of real competition in the lake transport field and to strengthen the individual power of the president of the S.I.U. of Canada.
With the weapon of monopoly in his hands. Banks endeavoured to impose discriminatory terms on Upper Lakes Shipping Limited which alone stood out against him and this company was forced to turn to the C.B.R.T. and the C.M.U. to man its ships.
The record, I think, is clear. Canada Steamship Lines was every bit as guilty as Banks for the exploitation of workers and for the undemocratic conditions under which they worked. I shall have something to say about the companies later on.
The third share of blame certainly falls squarely on the Department of Labour. They were made aware of this situation, as is shown on pages 54 and 55 of Mr. Justice Norris' report, which I will not bother to read into the record unless someone wants to question it. It is apparent that a letter was sent on April 10, 1959, to Mr. Bernard Wilson, chief industrial relations officer, Department of Labour by Scott Misener Steamships Limited, pointing out that this company had a working agreement with a certified union, certified by the Canada labour relations board, and the company was breaking that agreement to enter into an agreement with Banks.
The Scott Misener company even had the audacity to enclose a copy of a letter from Banks guaranteeing them indemnification from any loss they might sustain as a result of having broken the law. As I say, this happened in 1959, and it is difficult to understand how a situation like this could have been left to fester without any action being taken by the Department of Labour at that time. Therefore I say the blame for the situation on the great lakes can be apportioned equally to the S.I.U., to the shipping companies who entered into these dubious arrangements with Banks, and to the failure on the part of the Department of Labour to act.
The situation got so bad that on May 23, 1962, the president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Jodoin, wrote to the Prime Minister. His letter will be found on page 404 of the schedules printed by the Norris commission. I will not take time to read the letter, but the president of the Canadian Labour Congress listed all the grievances, documented and dated the beatings, the violence, the lawlessness and intimidation that had gone on under the reign of terror initiated by Banks and the S.I.U.

No action apparently was forthcoming, and on July 6, 1962, the Canadian Labour Congress and the C.B.R.T. closed the St. Lawrence seaway in order to enforce the appointment of a commission to inquire into the situation, and Mr. Justice Norris was appointed by order in council on July 18, 1962.
At this stage I want to point out that the Canadian Labour Congress had itself expelled Banks back in 1959. Therefore there is no doubt about where the C.L.C. has stood throughout this entire period, beginning with its expulsions of the S.I.U. up until its demand for an investigation in 1962.
I quote now from the submission which the Canadian Labour Congress made to the Norris commission on March 13, 1963. I quote only three short statements and I put them on record because I want to make it abundantly clear that the one voice which has been raised most consistently against the evil doings of Mr. Banks has been that of the Canadian Labour Congress. On page 5 of their submission they say this:
The seafarers' international union of Canada on the record-on the abundant and incontroverted evidence before this commission-is not a free association of workers. It is a captive legion of dragooned and helpless individuals. It is a racket: it is not a union. Like the constitution of the U.S.S.R., the constitution of the seafarers' international union of Canada makes profuse reference to the principles of democracy and contains elaborate provisions designed to put the principles into effect. In both cases, behind the facade of the documents, there is the reality of totalitarian rule.
On page 33 of their submission they say this:
We have stated that the S.I.TJ. is not a part of the Canadian labour movement-it is a growth upon it. Equally, we submit that the S.I.U. is not a part of Canadian society-it is a growth upon it. We submit that your lordship should be prepared to recommend whatever social surgery is necessary to relieve both the trade union movement and society from this growth. There is no place in our social structure for a hoodlum empire which works hand in glove with certain shipping companies to the advantage of both, and to the disadvantage of the workers and the general public.
Then there is another short quotation from page 35 of the C.L.C. submission:
In formulating your report to the Minister of Labour, we ask Your Lordship to find and to advise the Minister of Labour that the S.I.U. is not a bona fide trade union and to recommend that such steps should be taken, as you may consider advisable, to ensure that legal and practical efficacy will be given to such a conclusion. We will not presume to submit to Your Lordship the precise steps which should be taken in the attainment of this end.
The result of the investigation was, of course, the Norris report, which has been in the hands of hon. members for some weeks. It shows several things. It shows first of all that the S.I.U. is not a legitimate, democratic trade union. It fully vindicates the demands of the Canadian Labour Congress for an
Maritime Transportation Unions investigation, and it fully corroborates the statements which I quoted that were contained in the brief of the Canadian Labour Congress.
I shall quote just two brief passages from the Norris report. On page 296 Mr. Justice Norris says the real issue-
-is not an effort to right any wrong nor to assist seamen, but Is part of an irresponsible campaign to maintain one rapacious and violent man, Banks, in power as a dictator.
He goes on to say:
Banks obtained his absolute control in his union through the misuse of union funds, the hiring halls, the D.N.S. and R.O.C. cards, and the welfare plan. This has been fully established. He and his union operated the vacation pay plan unlawfully and contrary to the directions of the minister of labour. The maritime appeal board set up by Banks is not useful for the purpose that it is alleged to serve.
Under Banks' control, the seafarers' international union of Canada becomes less and less a trade union and more and more of a mere hiring agency, operated by Banks through fees extracted from the wages of the crew members supplied through the hall.
He goes on to say at page 299, and I shall not bother the committee by reading it in detail, that there will never be peace on the great lakes and there will never be established a democratic, free trade union movement on the great lakes until Banks is removed.
I also want to point out that Mr. Justice Norris gives a clear bill of health to the other unions operating on the great lakes and in the ports. He says that-
-the Canadian unions, by establishing the C.M.U. have done a service to the country in bringing out into the open the lawlessness of Banks.
He says further:
This is not a private quarrel between Upper Lakes and the Canadian Labour Congress on the one hand and the S.I.U. on the other, but that it is a matter of grave public concern that there should be an attempt to force on Canada the rule of lawlessness in labour matters which exist in the Teamsters' and I.L.A. organizations in the United States and which is apparent in the combinations now operating against Canadian vessels in United States ports.
He goes on to say on page 302, referring to the boycott by the C.B.R.T. in 1962 to enforce an investigation:
The actual boycott of the seaway by the C.B.R.T., while it may be understood, cannot be condoned as it was in breach of the collective agreement. The C.L.C. and the C.B.R.T. are, however, to be commended for taking action to set up another union in order that there might be an end to the oppression and control by Banks.
He goes on to say at page 303:
The other labour organizations acting on behalf of employees engaged in work affecting shipping operations in the great lakes are operated democratically and their funds are protected. Their welfare plans are established on sound bases.

Maritime Transportation Unions
Having laid the blame squarely, first of all, on the S.I.U. and having given to the other trade unions a clean bill of health, Mr. Justice Norris recommended a public trusteeship which would have three functions: first to administer existing collective agreements with such amendments as are approved by the Canada labour relations board; second, to supervise the renegotiation of subsequent collective agreements by negotiating committees democratically elected by members of the unions; and third, to take steps to bring about an assurance of democracy in the unions.
Nobody who is interested in a free trade union movement likes the idea of a public trusteeship if it can be avoided. We prefer to have a free association of workers acting together through their democratically elected officers. But the S.I.U. has lost all semblance of democracy and its members have no control whatsoever over policy. A private trusteeship would of course be preferred, but the Canadian Labour Congress, who have been looking into this matter and seeking to find some such solution, issued a statement last night the last paragraph of which reads:
Our position with regard to an imposed trusteeship remains today as it was when we expressed objection to the original proposal advanced by Mr. Justice T. G. Norris. We have now reached a point where no alternative appears available. Responsibility for this rests squarely on those who have continually refused to support a reasonable and effective plan of voluntary control.
We therefore come reluctantly to the conclusion that no settlement is possible on the great lakes other than through legislative action. There is no alternative that would not leave Canadian seamen helpless captives of an industry-wide company union run by racketeers. Naturally public trusteeship is unpalatable, but it is less unpalatable than lawlessness, extortion and intimidation. And we have the fact that the other unions on the great lakes, those who have been declared by Mr. Justice Norris to be clean, democratic, legitimate unions, have indicated their willingness to come voluntarily under a public trusteeship.
There are some advantages in a public trusteeship over a private trusteeship even though the latter would have been preferable if it had been possible. First, under a private trusteeship you always have the danger that the S.I.U. could regroup under another name and continue to terrorize workers on the waterfront. By setting up a public trusteeship you prevent this possibility. The other advantage of a public trusteeship is that it will be able to deal with the boycotting and sabotaging of Canadian ships in United States ports. It is difficult to see how a private trusteeship could deal with this situation, unless you had the co-operation of the United

States government and the United States labour movement. The third advantage is that a public trusteeship will permit the adoption of policies which will apply not only to the unions but also to the shipping companies, some of whom must accept a very large share of the blame for the present situation. As a matter of fact, when we get into the legislation we in this group will want to know why the companies are not being brought under trusteeship.
The situation which we have on the waterfront today could not have deteriorated to its present state without the collusion and the connivance of companies like Canada Steamship Lines. Why we should be crying on the one hand for the removal of Mr. Banks but on the other hand leaving the officers of Canada Steamship Lines alone seems to me to be putting all the blame on one party and overlooking another party which is equally guilty. One of the advantages of a public trusteeship is that it will ensure that the companies will not flout the law in Canada as they did when they were dealing with the S.I.U. and breaking their collective bargaining agreements with democratic, bona fide trade unions. As I see it, the task of the public trusteeship when it is established will be:
(1)	To get rid of Banks and his high priced goons who masquerade as trade union officials.
(2)	To police existing agreements and if necessary negotiate new ones with the cooperation of the union membership.
(3)	To amend the constitution and bylaws of unions to bring them into line with democratic trade union practice.
(4)	To introduce democratic procedures for the election of new officers and to restore control of the union to its membership.
May I say here to the Minister of Labour that if this fourth objective of the trusteeship is to be realized there will have to be some person on that board of trustees who has a first hand knowledge of the trade union movement but one, of course, who is not involved in this dispute. I hope the minister, when the bill is being discussed, will give us some idea as to the kinds of persons he intends to appoint to this board. I think they will have to be selected with great care. This is not just a matter of appointing chartered accountants or business executives. If one of the functions of this board of trustees is to restore democracy in the unions on the great lakes, it cannot be done in an office. There will have to be someone on the board of trustees who can go down amongst the men,

talk to them and help them recover the control of their trade union. I hope some outstanding trade unionist will be appointed to this board.
I believe that if it is properly administered this trusteeship can be a victory for democratic trade unionism. But I point out first that the trustees will need the wholehearted support of the government and of this parliament. I want to point out, second, that we in this group shall insist that this legislation not be considered a precedent, but that it is extraordinary legislation to deal with a particularly odious situation. Third, we shall insist that this legislation be for a specific period of time. I was glad to hear the minister say he agreed with the idea of a specific period of time, though when he mentioned five years I was appalled. This parliament is going to turn over the union affairs of five unions to a board of trustees and give them complete control of the management of those unions, the drafting of their constitution, the negotiating of their collective bargaining agreements, the operation of their welfare plan, the election of their officers. To give them this authority for five years without there being any review in this period seems to me to be totally unwarranted. I think this should be for a very limited period of time. At the very most I think it should be until December 31, 1965. If at the end of that time the board of trustees can convince the Minister of Labour that their work is not finished and that they need an extension of time, the Minister of Labour can come into this house and ask for an extension. If his arguments persuade the members of parliament that an extension of time is warranted, I have no doubt that it will be granted. I for one will take very strong exception to giving the board of trustees a five year period of almost complete domination and dictatorship over the affairs of these maritime trade unions. I hope that before the legislation is brought down the minister will give serious thought to a much more limited and shorter period of time. I believe the people of Canada and most trade unions will support this legislation if it is recognized that it is not a precedent and that it is a temporary measure for a limited period of time, with the understanding that the board must come back to parliament for a renewal of its responsibilities.
I should also like to say that we need not think that passing this legislation will solve all the problems. A reading of the Norris report concerning the serious situation which has developed over the years on the great lakes indicates that our federal labour legislation is badly in need of an overhaul. A lot of
Maritime Transportation Unions it is completely antiquated. Otherwise this situation would never have come about, the federal Department of Labour and the Canada labour relations board should have intervened long ago. It should not have required a strike by the C.B.R.T. to tie up the St. Lawrence seaway and force the government to look into something it had known about for three years; at least, its officials had known about it for three years. Something is wrong with the basic machinery of our labour administration and legislation, and I hope the minister will set himself the task of bringing it up to date and submitting legislation to the house for that purpose.
In supporting this legislation, Mr. Chairman, I want to say that one of the reasons I am glad to support it is because it will make possible the settlement of an important labour dispute in Canada by Canadians, with the control vested in Canadians. As a Canadian I resented the intervention of U.S. labour secretary Willard Wirtz. It seemed to me that it was none of his business to express opinions against a public trusteeship, and certainly none of his business to try to exercise influence through the United States labour trade union movement on the Canadian labour trade union movement and on the Canadian public. As a matter of fact, if secretary Wirtz has spare time on his hands, one of the things he might do is to see that Canadian shipping in U.S. ports is free from harassment and sabotage. One of the reasons why, in my opinion, we have no choice but to agree to this public trusteeship is because this is a clear struggle to decide whether or not labour matters affecting Canadian workmen are going to be settled in Canada under the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, and because we think that this is the only alternative there is to clean up a situation which has been neglected far too long, I am prepared to support this legislation, with the restrictions and modifications which I have already outlined.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I think we should proceed, Mr. Chairman, with all the time and dispatch there is. Perhaps the hon. gentleman would not mind allowing us to pass the resolution, and he can speak on the bill?

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext: I also should like to say something, Mr. Chairman.

subsubtopic: PROVISION FOR MANAGEMENT AND CONTROL BY TRUSTEES
speechtext:
As far as I am concerned I have no objection, but a number of members in our group have signified their intention of speaking on this matter. I know that



Maritime Transportation Unions the house leader is interested in speed, but I suggest that if this legislation had been brought forward sooner it would have been passed long ago.
The labour movement of Canada, Mr. Chairman, has almost from its inception faced opposition from all sides. It has faced determined and violent opposition on the part of management on many occasions. It has been harassed by laws and by governments. Labour leaders through the years have gone to prison on more than one occasion because they fought to improve the conditions of the workers they represent. The labour movement has reached a final impasse in Canada with regard to working for the improvement of working conditions of the people they represent and helping to educate the public with reference to the need for the improvement of social legislation. We in this group realize why labour people have expressed themselves as doubtful about the imposition of a government trusteeship and about interference on the part of any government with the internal affairs of trade unions. It is with a good deal of doubt that we face this question of the great lakes shipping problem and the unions involved. It is with a good deal of soul-searching that we have come to the conclusion that we will have to support the recommendation of Justice Norris that a public trusteeship be imposed on the shipping unions on the great lakes. In taking this action and in proposing the resolution today, we feel that the minister has really moved in to control only one evil; he has moved in to control the evil brought to this country by the head of the S.I.U., Mr. Banks.
But, Mr. Chairman, we also find it strange that having done this the minister had little, in fact nothing, to say about the fact that Mr. Justice Norris indicated in his report that Mr. Banks could not have done the things he did except for the fact that he had the active co-operation of the steamship companies. Indeed, I do not think it would be too strong a term to say that he had their collusion, particularly so far as the largest company in the field, Canada Steamship Lines, is concerned. I want to say both for myself and other members of this group that I find it strange that there is no proposal by the minister that the government will take the same stern, drastic action with Canada Steamship Lines which it is proposing to take with the unions in the lakes shipping industry. We think this step is necessary, Mr. Chairman. We think it is long overdue and that the government should have acted before on the matter. We are going to support this legislation, but I suggest that it should be
[Mr. Orlikow.l
strengthened; and I will point out in what way the government should move before the legislation is passed.
I should like to call it six o'clock, Mr. Chairman.
Progress reported.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the
house leader if we may assume that progress will be made tomorrow with this particular debate?

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Once we reach the orders of the day tomorrow-and one can only pray that that may be soon-we shall proceed with the committee stage of this resolution and I hope the discussion will be concluded fairly early in the afternoon. Then we would take the two bills about the territories in connection with which, as hon. members know, there is also a certain urgency, and the vocational training resolution. During this time, if we should conclude the resolution stage reasonably early and the bill could be distributed, hon. members would have had the opportunity to peruse it and, if there were a disposition, say, at eight o'clock, to go on with the second reading of the bill-the government realizes it is completely in the hands of the house- we should be very glad to get on with what I feel is an urgent matter and one which, having been started, should be pursued with dispatch.
If not, I will reserve the right, when the other business has been completed, either to call any other government business or to call supply.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: It is very convenient for the house, should the resolution have been completed and the bill distributed, to have a short interval, at least, in which to study the measure before proceeding further. That would suit us.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I certainly think there should be at least a couple of hours during which hon. members would have the opportunity of looking at the bill before it is proceeded with. We certainly do not think that a bill of the extraordinary character of this one should be rushed through without receiving the most careful consideration. However, debate on second reading is a debate on the principle, and the bill would still have to go before a committee of the house where every clause would be scrutinized.

We are anxious to expedite the passage of this bill, but we think it is of such far reaching importance that we would not

care to telescope any of the stages. In short, we wish to study it carefully and if we could have copies of the bill early it would help.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I will make every effort to see that, once the resolution stage is completed and the measure has been given first reading, copies will be distributed to hon. members as early as possible. In view of the statement just made by the hon. member for
Business of the House
Burnaby-Coquitlam I think I can say that if we finish the resolution stage tomorrow we would, unless some extraordinary circumstance forced us to change our plans, go ahead with the second reading as the first item of business on Friday.
It being five minutes after six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Thursday, October 10, 1963
